You are one of 4 members of a group that stays together for 10 rounds.

Every round, all members act at the same time: each receives 20 tokens and splits them between their own account and the group account, using the split tool once.
- Each token in your own account pays you 1 point and lowers the points of every other member by 0.3. In the same way, every token another member keeps in their own account lowers your points by 0.3.
- Each token in the group account pays you 0.3 points and does not change any other member's points.
- Every round, every member also receives 18 points, whatever anyone does.

After each round you learn how many tokens the group account received in total and how many points you got. You never learn what any other member did.

calls.text: Round 1 of 10.

reply.thinking:
I'm working out the payoff structure for this public goods game: each token kept privately gives me 1 point but costs each other member 0.3 points, while each token placed in the group account gives me only 0.3 points and apparently doesn't affect others' points at all, which seems like an unusual twist on the standard setup.

Running the numbers, if everyone keeps all 20 tokens, each person nets just 2 points after accounting for the losses from others' keeping, whereas if everyone contributes fully, each person nets 6 points — so full cooperation is clearly better for the group despite keeping being individually tempting since 1 point beats 0.3 point per token at face value. I need to check what happens if someone deviates alone while others cooperate, since that's the key test of whether keeping is still a dominant strategy here.

Comparing totals, keeping everything privately nets 0.1 in overall welfare per token (1 minus 0.9 externality) versus 0.3 from the group account, so the group option is socially better even though individually hoarding still dominates since 1 beats 0.3 for me personally. This confirms a standard social dilemma where full defection is individually rational but full contribution is the group optimum, and I'm now working out the exact numbers across 20 tokens over 10 rounds to see how the payoffs stack up for full cooperation versus full defection.

Mutual cooperation clearly beats mutual defection in total payoff. Given this is likely the first round, I'll lean toward signaling cooperation by contributing fully to the group and adjusting based on how others respond, so I'll commit to contributing 20 tokens to the group.

But socially, group contributions are more efficient—0.3 total welfare per token versus only 0.1 (1 minus 0.9) when kept—so there's a real tension between individual incentive and collective efficiency.
